## The approach

SpecStory Cloud should adopt Vercel's project model wholesale, with one adaptation for the fact that our "connect" is a local sync rather than a deploy. Two ideas carry the whole design:

> **1. A workspace belongs to a *scope* (a personal account or an org), not to a user. A personal account is just a scope with one member.**
>
> **2. A workspace's identity is its own server-assigned UUID. The git repo is a *binding* that routes sessions to it — the preferred binding when it exists, but never the identity itself.**

Ownership moving from user → scope is what turns "two teammates on one repo" from two workspaces into one. Identity being the UUID (not the git id) is what lets a project exist before it has a repo, gain one later, and be shared without a repo at all.

The new required piece these force into existence: **the CLI must resolve which *scope* to sync into**, not just which project — the direct analog of Vercel's `.vercel/project.json { orgId, projectId }`. Add a scope/`org_id` field to `.specstory/.project.json`. Default is the personal scope; binding to an org is deliberate.

## The principles

1. **Ownership is a scope.** Replace `owner_id: user` with an owner that is either a personal scope or an org. Access to an org workspace is *derived from org membership*; `user_permissions` evolves from "the sharing table" into "memberships + personal-workspace shares."

2. **Identity is the UUID; the repo is a binding.** Uniqueness is `(binding, scope)`, and a binding is one of three kinds:

   | Binding | Derived from | Collides across users? | Role |
   |---|---|---|---|
   | **Portable** (`git_id`, later maybe GitHub node id) | shared remote URL | Yes, by design | Enables *automatic* grouping |
   | **Explicit link** (workspace UUID) | server-assigned, written to `.project.json` | Yes — everyone stores the same UUID | Grouping when there's nothing to derive |
   | **Local** (`workspace_id` path hash) | absolute path | No | A per-machine *default* only |

   Auto-collapse (`upsert onConflict`) happens **only on portable bindings**. A workspace can carry several bindings at once and gain or swap them over its life without losing history.

3. **Same repo → N independent workspaces across scopes is normal.** A portable binding is unique *within* a scope, never globally. Personal, Org A, and Org B can each have a workspace for the same repo simultaneously, fully isolated.

4. **Git-less projects are first-class.** They just can't be auto-discovered, so they're joined by explicit UUID link — exactly like Vercel. The path hash is only a local default, never a sharing key.

5. **Membership grants access; leaving revokes it; the resource stays with the scope.** You never take the team's workspace with you.

6. **Merging and moving between scopes are always explicit acts, never side effects** of joining or leaving. They're lossless because sessions carry author provenance.

## The answers

| Scenario | Answer |
|---|---|
| **Same org, same repo, both sync** | **One workspace** — provided both CLIs are bound to the org scope. The `git_id` already matches; the upsert key `(git_id, org)` collapses them. The moving part is scope selection, not repo matching. |
| **Not same org → both join org O** | **Nothing automatic.** Their two personal workspaces stay personal and private. Joining a team never migrates personal projects. Collaboration requires *explicitly bringing the repo into O.* |
| **…and when they bring it into O** | They converge on the single `(git_id, O)` workspace. Because sessions carry **author/device/agent provenance**, this is a lossless *merge* — both people's sessions re-parent into the one workspace, each still attributed. No "who wins." |
| **One of them leaves O** | Everything synced into O's workspace **stays with O**; the leaver loses cloud access. They lose nothing real — their local `.specstory/history/` is the source of truth they always keep. (Last member/owner → normal org lifecycle: transfer or delete-cascade.) |
| **Two orgs, separate workspaces, same repo** | **Fully independent and expected.** `(git_id, A)` and `(git_id, B)` are different workspaces with their own members, sessions, and access. `git_id` is not globally unique. |
| **Non-git folder → becomes a GitHub repo** | The workspace **keeps its UUID identity and gains `git_id` as a new portable binding** — it does not spawn a fresh workspace. Existing contributors were already attached (by explicit link or their local path hash); the repo arriving simply makes the workspace *auto-discoverable* so new teammates can join by derivation. History carries forward untouched. |
| **Git-less project shared across people/machines** | Joined by **explicit UUID link** written into each contributor's `.specstory/.project.json` (the `.vercel/project.json { projectId }` analog). Path-hash `workspace_id` can't do this — it never collides across machines — so it stays a local default only. |

## What this commits you to in the schema (when you build it)

Three enabling changes, in priority order:

1. **Sessions get author provenance** (`authored_by`, `device_id`, `agent_name` at the session level). This is the keystone — without it, merges and departures are lossy and unattributable.
2. **Owner becomes a scope** (`organizations` table + nullable `workspaces.org_id`, or polymorphic `(owner_type, owner_id)`); uniqueness moves to `(binding, scope)`.
3. **`project_id` becomes a rebindable binding set, not the identity** — support attaching a `git_id` to an existing workspace, plus a rebind operation the CLI triggers on the git transition. (Write down the known limitation now: URL-hash bindings don't survive a GitHub rename/transfer/fork; the sturdier future binding is GitHub's immutable repo node id, via the same alias machinery.)

The one decision that stays yours: **default sync scope + how the CLI picks it.** My recommendation — default to personal (privacy-safe, keeps desktop sync frictionless), make org binding an explicit opt-in, and auto-group only *within* a chosen scope.

# Org Workspaces — Design Point of View

**Status:** thinking / not yet implemented
**Scope:** the relationship between cloud users, cloud orgs, cloud workspaces, and CLI projects

This document takes a point of view on how organizations should work in SpecStory
Cloud, modeled on Vercel's project system, and works several hard scenarios through
that point of view. It is a design stance, not an implementation plan.

---

## Background: how it works today

A workspace today is **user-scoped**: one row per `(project_id, owner_id)` pair.

- `workspaces.project_id` — a client-generated identifier from the CLI.
- `workspaces.owner_id` — the Clerk user id of the owner.
- Unique constraint on `(project_id, owner_id)` → exactly one workspace per user per project.
- `sessions.workspace_id` foreign-keys into `workspaces`; a session belongs to one workspace.
- `user_permissions` grants other users access to a workspace.

On the CLI side, the `project_id` sent to the cloud is resolved in
`pkg/cloud/sync.go` as `git_id ?? workspace_id`:

- **`git_id`** — hash of the normalized git origin remote URL. **Intentionally collides**
  across users and machines (Alice's clone and Bob's clone hash the same). This
  collision is the mechanism that lets "same repo → same workspace" happen.
- **`workspace_id`** — hash of the canonical absolute path. **Never meaningfully collides**;
  it is a per-machine, per-path local fingerprint.

The key consequence: because ownership is keyed on the user, two teammates on the same
repo resolve the same `git_id` but different `owner_id`, and therefore get **two separate
workspaces** today.

---

## The approach

Adopt Vercel's project model wholesale, with one adaptation for the fact that our
"connect" is a local sync rather than a deploy. Two ideas carry the whole design:

> **1. A workspace belongs to a _scope_ (a personal account or an org), not to a user.
> A personal account is just a scope with one member.**
>
> **2. A workspace's identity is its own server-assigned UUID. The git repo is a
> _binding_ that routes sessions to it — the preferred binding when it exists, but never
> the identity itself.**

Ownership moving from user → scope is what turns "two teammates on one repo" from two
workspaces into one. Identity being the UUID (not the git id) is what lets a project
exist before it has a repo, gain one later, and be shared without a repo at all.

The new required piece these force into existence: **the CLI must resolve which _scope_
to sync into**, not just which project — the direct analog of Vercel's
`.vercel/project.json { orgId, projectId }`. Add a scope / `org_id` field to
`.specstory/.project.json`. Default is the personal scope; binding to an org is deliberate.

---

## The principles

### 1. Ownership is a scope

Replace `owner_id: user` with an owner that is either a personal scope or an org. Access
to an org workspace is *derived from org membership*; `user_permissions` evolves from
"the sharing table" into "memberships + personal-workspace shares."

### 2. Identity is the UUID; the repo is a binding

Uniqueness is `(binding, scope)`, and a binding is one of three kinds:

| Binding | Derived from | Collides across users? | Role |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Portable** (`git_id`, later maybe GitHub node id) | shared remote URL | Yes, by design | Enables *automatic* grouping |
| **Explicit link** (workspace UUID) | server-assigned, written to `.project.json` | Yes — everyone stores the same UUID | Grouping when there's nothing to derive |
| **Local** (`workspace_id` path hash) | absolute path | No | A per-machine *default* only |

Auto-collapse (`upsert onConflict`) happens **only on portable bindings**. A workspace
can carry several bindings at once and gain or swap them over its life without losing
history.

### 3. Same repo → N independent workspaces across scopes is normal

A portable binding is unique *within* a scope, never globally. Personal, Org A, and Org B
can each have a workspace for the same repo simultaneously, fully isolated.

### 4. Git-less projects are first-class

They just can't be auto-discovered, so they're joined by explicit UUID link — exactly
like Vercel. The path hash is only a local default, never a sharing key.

### 5. Membership grants access; leaving revokes it; the resource stays with the scope

You never take the team's workspace with you.

### 6. Merging and moving between scopes are always explicit acts

Never side effects of joining or leaving. They're lossless because sessions carry author
provenance.

---

## The answers

| Scenario | Answer |
|---|---|
| **Same org, same repo, both sync** | **One workspace** — provided both CLIs are bound to the org scope. The `git_id` already matches; the upsert key `(git_id, org)` collapses them. The moving part is scope selection, not repo matching. |
| **Not same org → both join org O** | **Nothing automatic.** Their two personal workspaces stay personal and private. Joining a team never migrates personal projects. Collaboration requires *explicitly bringing the repo into O.* |
| **…and when they bring it into O** | They converge on the single `(git_id, O)` workspace. Because sessions carry **author / device / agent provenance**, this is a lossless *merge* — both people's sessions re-parent into the one workspace, each still attributed. No "who wins." |
| **One of them leaves O** | Everything synced into O's workspace **stays with O**; the leaver loses cloud access. They lose nothing real — their local `.specstory/history/` is the source of truth they always keep. (Last member / owner → normal org lifecycle: transfer or delete-cascade.) |
| **Two orgs, separate workspaces, same repo** | **Fully independent and expected.** `(git_id, A)` and `(git_id, B)` are different workspaces with their own members, sessions, and access. `git_id` is not globally unique. |
| **Non-git folder → becomes a GitHub repo** | The workspace **keeps its UUID identity and gains `git_id` as a new portable binding** — it does not spawn a fresh workspace. Existing contributors were already attached (by explicit link or their local path hash); the repo arriving simply makes the workspace *auto-discoverable* so new teammates can join by derivation. History carries forward untouched. |
| **Git-less project shared across people / machines** | Joined by **explicit UUID link** written into each contributor's `.specstory/.project.json` (the `.vercel/project.json { projectId }` analog). Path-hash `workspace_id` can't do this — it never collides across machines — so it stays a local default only. |

---

## What this commits us to in the schema

Three enabling changes, in priority order.

1. **Sessions get author provenance** — `authored_by` (Clerk user), `device_id`,
   `agent_name` at the session level (some already arrives in the CLI's metadata payload).
   This is the keystone: without it, merges and departures are lossy and unattributable.

2. **Owner becomes a scope** — an `organizations` table + nullable `workspaces.org_id`
   (null = personal, owned by `owner_id`), or a polymorphic `(owner_type, owner_id)`.
   Uniqueness moves to `(binding, scope)`.

3. **`project_id` becomes a rebindable binding set, not the identity** — support attaching
   a `git_id` to an existing workspace, plus a rebind operation the CLI triggers on the
   git transition.

   > **Known limitation to record now:** URL-hash bindings do not survive a GitHub
   > rename / transfer / fork (the URL changes → a new `git_id`). The sturdier future
   > binding is GitHub's immutable repo node id, carried through the same alias machinery.

---

## The one decision that stays open

**Default sync scope, and how the CLI picks it.**

Recommendation, straight from Vercel: **default to the personal scope** (privacy-safe,
keeps desktop sync frictionless), make org binding an explicit opt-in, and auto-group
only *within* a chosen scope. The tension to resolve is that Vercel's linking is
deliberate (`vercel link`) whereas our desktop sync is meant to be automatic:
auto-grouping *within* a scope is fine, but *choosing the org scope* is where we should
keep a human in the loop.
